title: They didn’t stack stones because it looked beautiful.
paragraphs:
They didn’t stack stones because it looked beautiful.
They stacked stones because they knew something terrifying…
In Joshua 4, God does something powerful—He parts the Jordan River. Not a trick. Not a symbol. A real river. Flowing. Stopping. Standing still.

Mud becomes dust.
Chaos becomes a pathway.
Fear becomes movement.
But right after the miracle… God gives a command that feels almost strange:
“Take twelve stones from the middle of the river… and carry them with you.”

Not celebrate.
Not shout.
Not build a palace.
Because God knows something about the human heart that we often refuse to admit:
We forget Him… even after He saves us.

You cried out in that dark season.
You begged God to come through.
You promised, “Lord, if You do this… I will never forget.”

He made a way.
He healed.
He restored.
He carried you through something you had no strength to survive.

Life is “normal” again.
The urgency faded.
The fire cooled.
“In the future, when your children ask you, ‘What do these stones mean?’ tell them… what the Lord has done.”

Because questions will come.
Doubts will rise.
Generations will forget what they did not witness.
A physical reminder of a spiritual reality.
A visible memory of invisible grace.
Each stone came from the place that once looked impossible.

The place where fear was loudest.
The place where turning back felt safer.
The place where death seemed closer than promise.
And that’s exactly where God said:
Because your greatest testimony will always come from your deepest struggle.
Now here’s the truth most people won’t say:

Moments God carried you.
Prayers He answered.
Battles you didn’t win—but He did.

That night you almost gave up.
That sin you couldn’t break—but somehow you walked away.
That pain that should’ve destroyed you—but didn’t.
But if you don’t mark those moments…

You’ll call it coincidence.
You’ll call it luck.
You’ll call it “timing.”
God’s miracle becomes your memory glitch.
This is why remembrance is not optional in the life of a believer.

Because forgetting leads to drifting…
And drifting leads to distance…
And distance leads to disbelief.
And then comes the greatest shift.
In Luke 22:19, Jesus took bread, broke it, and said:
Because the greatest danger to your faith is not persecution…

We remember who hurt us.
We remember what went wrong.
We remember the betrayal, the failure, the shame.

We forget how lost we were.
We forget how far He brought us.
We forget that without Jesus—we would still be drowning.
On the cross, He saw everything.

Every sin.
Every secret.
Every failure you try to hide.

He carried it.
He bore it.
He paid for it.
So now the question is not:
Not with rocks—but with a life that refuses to forget.

Write it down.
Speak it out.
Tell your children.
Tell your friends.
Tell your own soul when it starts to doubt.
Go back to the cross daily.
Because a faith that forgets… fades.
One day, someone will look at your life and ask:
And you won’t need theology alone.

You’ll point to your scars.
Your story.
Your survival.
“Let me tell you what He did.”
Because the same God who parted the river…
Is still making a way for you today.
